Supported by By Sui-Lee Wee and Aie Balagtas See Photographs by Jes Aznar Reporting from the village of Manabayucan in the Philippines and the capital, Manila In May, Roseller Rodriguez, a mayor in the Philippines, was startled to learn from news reports that American officials had arrived in his district to start an artificial intelligence hub. He saw a video of senior American and Filipino officials standing on a makeshift stage, unveiling a new initiative called Pax Silica. Mr. Rodriguez had not been invited. Nor had he ever heard about the hub. Was it a data center? Where would the water and electricity come from? What would happen to the farmers living there? Months later, he says he has few answers. “I’m not concerned with the geopolitics of Pax Silica,” Mr. Rodriguez said in his office in the municipality of Capas. “My problem is Pax Silica will be built in our community.” Last December, the United States started Pax Silica to unite partners around A.I. supply chains independent of China. The initiative is part of President Trump’s effort to counter Beijing’s economic and technological influence. Trump administration officials have cast it as a 21st-century successor to “Pax Americana,” the era of relative peace among major powers after World War II.
